title: Necessity of sinning does not remove essential liberty
source_text: XXXIX. Quamvis enim absente gratia, Homo sit peccati servus, ut scriptura loquitur, & quicquid agat non possit nisi peccare: ista tamen male agendi necessitas naturalem arbitrii ejus libertatem non tollit. Libertas enim illa quae essentialis est omni agenti intellectu & voluntate praedito, non consistit in eo ut quis indifferens sit ad bene vel male agendum, & parem ad utrumque facultatem habeat. Alioqui nec daemones in inferno, nec Angeli in coelo libere operarentur, cum illi quidem ad male agendum, hi vero contra ad bene agendum sint determinati. Verum in eo sita est ista naturalis arbitrii libertas, ut quis agat non coactus, nec etiam bruto naturae impulsu, sed praevio mentis judicio & deliberatione eligat quod ipsi lubet & videtur. Adeoque libertas illa opponitur coactioni, & naturali, seu brutae determinationi, minime vero servituti peccati, quae non obstat quominus homo, dum peccat, deliberate agat, & ex rationis propriae dictamine, absque ulla coactione, & naturali seu bruta determinatione.
pass_a_gloss: XXXIX. For although with grace absent, Man be the servant of sin, as scripture speaks, and whatever he does cannot but sin: that necessity however of acting badly does not take away the natural liberty of his choice. For that liberty which is essential to every agent endowed with intellect and will, does not consist in this that one be indifferent to acting well or badly, and have an equal faculty for both. Otherwise neither the demons in hell, nor the Angels in heaven would act freely, since those indeed to acting badly, these on the contrary to acting well are determined. But in this is placed that natural liberty of choice, that one act not compelled, nor yet by brute impulse of nature, but with previous judgement of mind and deliberation choose what pleases and seems good to him. And so that liberty is opposed to coercion, and to natural, or brute determination, but by no means to the servitude of sin, which does not prevent that man, while he sins, act deliberately, and from the dictate of his own reason, without any coercion, and natural or brute determination.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXXIX. Without grace man is the servant of sin, as Scripture says, and whatever he does he cannot help sinning. Yet this necessity of doing evil does not take away the natural freedom of his choice. The freedom that belongs essentially to every agent with intellect and will does not consist in being indifferent between acting well and acting badly, with an equal power for either. Otherwise neither the demons in hell nor the angels in heaven would act freely, since the demons are fixed on doing evil and the angels, conversely, on doing good.

That natural freedom of choice consists rather in acting without compulsion and without any brute impulse of nature, choosing what one pleases and thinks fit after a prior judgement and deliberation of the mind. So this freedom is opposed to coercion and to natural or brute determination, but not at all to the bondage of sin. That bondage does not stop a man, when he sins, from acting deliberately and at the dictate of his own reason, without any coercion and without natural or brute determination.
